b: 99% of the time a person comes across your art, whether online or in-person, you get a tiny fraction of their attention. At home, people are scrolling on platforms that encourage them to move on and find the next dopamine hit. They were probably supposed to be doing something else entirely and forgot, once they picked up the phone! Now, they’ve accidentally stumbled on your drawing between a political ad and a recipe video.

At most events, folks walk by carrying on conversations, navigating, texting their friend back about lunch, all while passing dozens or hundreds of spaces crying for their attention. Hopefully, occasionally, your art will win out over that cacophony, and someone will slow down and look.
If we are lucky, they are intrigued and we get the opportunity to show them more. Maybe they follow our work, join the mailing list, or visit again at a future event.
Do we just…show them more art? Show them more times?
Recently, I’ve been reflecting on the barriers that exist between seeing art, and falling in love with it.
I have a friend who loves art, collects art, thinks about art, and increasingly over the last few years, makes art. Most of our mutual artist friends don’t know about that last part.

I feel privileged that he shows me the art he’s working on. I get the impression he thinks I’m blowing smoke when I have nice thoughts to share about his art. I’m not. I don’t have nice things to say because what he’s making is prodigious, but because it’s interesting, and I feel personally invested. Why is that?

In the book ‘Art and Fear,’ by David Bayles and Ted Orland, they say of the early stages of an artist’s journey, “Until your ship comes in, the only people who really care about your work are those who care about you personally…They will always care about your work, if not because it is great, because it is yours.”

Most often, the aesthetic distinction and consistency of a body of work gives us reason to stop and lean in. In other words, you like what it looks like, so you look longer. You see things you didn’t notice before, and maybe you’re driven to learn more about the artist, the process, or the title of the piece. Leaning in and learning more fosters a deeper connection with art.
Initial appeal usually proceeds getting to know art, but it isn’t necessary.

It is a common phenomenon to find that we like an artist’s work more after we get to know them. Sometimes, it happens because we learn something curious about the art, perhaps about the process, the meaning in the work, or hidden elements. It is fascinating that art that didn’t appeal to us at all before can change so suddenly, when we slow down to appreciate it and learn more.

Much of the art my kids have made was destined for the garbage. There’s just so much of it! But the art that gets saved is not the art that is prettier or shows technical potential, it’s the art that calls back to a silly joke they told practically every day in that period of their life. Or, it’s from that few weeks when they were obsessed with making pop-up books. It’s the one that has a genuine piece of them in it, and I am able to value that artwork above the others because I know those stories.

If art appreciation can circumvent aesthetic appeal, then it is very possible for art to be genuinely loved while technical skills are still developing. Often, the artistic journey is a part of the story of the artwork. My friend was hesitant to show his new work in a setting filled with friends, but I’m confident they would all be very interested to follow along in his artistic journey.

I was thinking about this a lot at the IX Art Show last week, as so many friends and colleagues gather to exhibit a large variety of artwork. The Gen Con and Dragoncon Art Shows are held in high esteem, but IX is unique because there is time to slow down and space to get close, to lean in and get to know the art. It is one of the very few places where art gets full attention. With no hurry, we can chat about our inspiration, the way we create the work, and why we make the art. These are invaluable for developing a deeper connection with artwork, and I’m grateful to get to know art and artists better there, and have a chance to fall in love with their art.
IX Arts 2026 is over now, so how do we carry that through the rest of the year?
I’m still working on that, but I think we must use the low-attention, multiple exposures we get online and at events wisely.

Many artists who exhibit at conventions put stories, poetry, or additional context on the back of their prints. This is a wonderful way to help people who were attracted to the aesthetic of the artwork develop a deeper relationship with it even after they’ve gone home. I think we may benefit from displaying the titles of our artwork clearly and choosing titles that enhance either the viewer’s understanding or their curiosity.

As for online, I think we artists are quick to turn up our noses at video ‘content,’ but videos are an effective way to help people lean in, spend a bit more time, and maybe get to know the art. They can be used to tell a story…a jpeg rarely pulls that off. Perhaps we could also be using our mailing lists not to advertise or announce, but to connect and tell more. It feels risky in the same way sharing art for the first time does: you feel uniquely exposed to judgement. Sincerity is difficult, especially when you can’t see the people you’re sharing with. But, that is what art is good for.
In what ways do you let your art be known?
